Billy Bauer

Guitarist Billy Bauer defines the word versatility. His career has included work with big bands, small swing combos and experimental jazz ensembles. He was born in New York on November 14, 1915 and learned the banjo at an early age.

Billy was able to use his music to work during the depression years and became a full time musician by his early twenties. He played in Woody Herman’s first Herd and with a long list of great jazz soloists, including Lee Konitz, Lennie Tristano, Benny Goodman and J.J. Johnson. Billy was a member of the Metronome All Stars from 1947-53 and was on staff with the NBC Orchestra.
He has authored a book entitled Sideman, and shares his experience in the world of jazz with students at his guitar studio on Long Island.
Billy was interviewed in New York City on March 22, 1998, by Monk Rowe, Director of the Fillius Jazz Archive.

We are filming today for the Hamilton College Jazz Archive in New York City. And I am really pleased to have Billy Bauer as my guest, who has been playing guitar for many years, and braved some inclement weather to be with us this morning. So I really appreciate it.
This is a cool day.
A cool guy and a cool day. I would like to ask you first about your guitar institute that you’re working on, your guitar business, your school.

Well it isn’t a big school, but what I do, I mean if I had to earn a living I couldn’t do it. But being the way I am, like at this part of my life, I like to see people and how they want to do things, these fellas take — some of them throw away everything. They think they’re going to be big stars or something. And they make their own record dates and they put everything they’ve got into this. So I try to tell them, you know, go ahead. It’s your turn to roll the dice. And then they say how did you — I says don’t do what I did. You know you’ve got your own life and I generally, when they get doing it they want to copy, and I try to tell them listen to other people that came before, like Lester Young or somebody like that, and sing their part. Don’t play it. Because on guitar, I don’t know if you’re familiar with guitar, but guitar, you get set fingerings and you’re really not improvising, you’re playing the same fingers. You know like for instance I say do you know all your scales? This is the first time they come. Either they say no or yes. But if they say yes, I say well all right, play it. So they play it. I say play it in the fifth position. They play in the fifth position but they just move up, instead of playing G they’re up like the B flat key but it’s the same fingering. So I try to explain to them that they’re playing their finger patterns — not that you can get away, guitar is a very, the fingerboard is odd. Like to read. © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-
So when you said that they’re just moving their fingers up a few positions and then playing that they don’t know the notes that they’re playing? Is that what you’re saying?

That’s right. They’ve got a finger pattern. Oh I know it’s a third — they can hear it — but they don’t know. So I say now if you’re going to come to me, do you want to learn how to read? And when they say yes, then I say well then you have to know where everything is. And some of them are piano players and saxophone, violin, they can read music. But they can’t find it on the guitar. See so that’s my little project, is to shows them different ways of learning the guitar, doing it in the head, that they can sing in their head. Anyway, what was that question?
We’re talking about — how many students does your business have right now?

Oh it does vary, about I guess most of the time it’s around eighteen, something like that. If I teach three hours or four hours a day, you see, I’m losing my voice now. I had to go the doctor last year because I used to lose my voice so much I couldn’t talk because I sing with them. [scats] All that kind of singing. See so I’m doing that all day and he says there’s nothing wrong, like you’ve not got anything wrong like cancer of the throat, but you’ve got weak whatever this is called, throat muscles.
Larynx?

Yeah. Like they’re weak. So that’s why everybody recommends — I say hello, they say oh Billy. And I don’t know them that well. See so I’ve got a very distinct sound, not that it’s good but it’s different. Well anyway.
Well you said an interesting thing before, they ask you well how did you do it, and you say well don’t do what I did. But let’s talk about what you did.

All right. Well the reason I give them, they say well you know like you say listen to Lester or Charlie or one of them guys. They says but that would be imitating. I says you can never imitate the same. Because they says what do you mean, we could play it. I says you see that? What am I showing you?
Your thumb.
Yeah. And a fingerprint. Every one of us has got a different fingerprint see. So I tell them that. So don’t be afraid, you ain’t going to sound like them.
Even if you try you’re not going to.
Even if you try. See and one time when I was, well you know I did a lot of different kinds of things. I was in big time but I wrote a book you know.
I know you did.

Sideman. Well that’s what I probably was all my life. You know, even if I was the leader I was still, when I led the group it was like, you know, if Clark Terry was there, he’d be the leader for that night. Well anyway, what was I saying?
Well I wanted to talk about, you said an interesting thing— © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-
I hope you have a lot of cuts.

Oh we can cut and snip if we want. But you said an interesting thing about how some of the younger players come to you and they make their own record dates and the whole thing. Would it have occurred to you, when you were let’s say 21, to go out and make your own record?

No. I didn’t think of that at all. But that’s the way the world is today. But then again I’m saying in the beginning, a record date, was like I didn’t even have a place and I had an old victrola. You know so records was like — I could go back so far, that radio wasn’t even – that’s a long time.
Well I want to actually. Let’s see it all started in 1915 in November, right?
Yeah.
You were born in New York?
Yeah. I was born in the Bronx.
And did you have a musical environment in your house?

Well see when these questions are asked of me, I don’t know. It seemed — now maybe it was just my household or my family or mother, but when we all got together for anything, like a dinner or a party, we all sang. You know that was the entertainment they sung [sings] “by the old mill stream.” And you sing that.
[Billy & Monk sing together]
You see? We all used to do that.
You were harmonizing.
Yeah, but I didn’t know.
It was part of your life at that time.

Yeah. Well everybody, every corner had like a little quartet, I think they put a name like the Barber Shop Quartet, but everybody did that. And the only instrument we had at that time was one of these piano rolls, and they had the lyrics on them as they come down. So we all stand around the piano and sing. And my mother played a little piano. And my father, well I never seen him perform, I seen him do it in the house then. But he was called Harry, his stage name supposedly was Harry Nelson. He says he sings, and then he’d come out and he’d do the amateur hours and get the hook. If he got the hook he’d get four dollars. If he just stayed in he’d get two dollars. If you got the hook the hook means that you’re so rotten and everybody said get him off, and that big hook would come out and grab you. So if they didn’t have anybody, they’d pay you to be the hook.
That’s good. So was that considered vaudeville?
Well you mean my father? Well that was Amateur Night that I’m talking about. But it was vaudeville. There was nothing else but vaudeville, and the movies was silent movies.
How much did it cost to get into the movies when you were a kid? © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

Oh gee, well now we used to call it a nickelette. So that was just the movies. But a vaudeville show was probably about 25 or 30 cents or something. I know it’s hard to believe. Well whenever anybody says — you know these young fellas, they go out and they do these club dates, and I says well how— He says you’ll never get, like you can’t earn a living. I says well how much do you get when you do these? Well he says $150. And they’ve got two or three over the weekend. I says that’s quite a lot. They says no, that ain’t no good, you get with the big offices, you do good. You know he says they’re gypping me. So I don’t know what to say. So I tell them, I says lookit, when I was young, what was a postal stamp? Not so far back, like two cents, right? Then it went up to three cents, everybody went wild. Now, 32 cents. That’s the difference with your money.
That’s right. What did your father do for a living?

He was a printer. He was really a song and dance man like I said, and he made, there was an audition — I wasn’t born about this time but he’d tell me that the audition was Ned Wayburn “School Days.” It got to be a big Broadway show. And they went up to Ossining, New York to break it in. And he made it as one of the guys in the cast, not the star. And as he went up to Ossining, which isn’t far from the Bronx, and his father told him if he could quit for show business was out. My grandfather, he thought that that was bad. So he says if you don’t, you ain’t got no place there, get out on your own. So my father got afraid, and come back and my grandfather was a printer, he became a printer. And he tried to do, later he tried to do the same thing with me. You know like because I started when I was nine. I broke my leg, my father bought me a ukulele while the girl pushed me around in a baby carriage, they didn’t have no big things, they just got an old baby carriage. And I was laid up for a couple of months with this big cast, you know you had a cast on your leg. You mind me telling you all this?
No I want to hear this.

So to keep me busy, he gave me a ukulele. At that time Harold Teen and Cliff Edwards, Ukulele Ike. And they’d play “five foot two, eyes of blue, koochie, koochie—” and that kind of thing. And for some reason I learned a couple of chords, and by the time my leg was better at the end of the summer, me and my cousin went on to summer school, the two ukuleles, we’d practice all day, and we got out there. Well I have this in my book you know. And you mind me telling you?
Please.

They pushed us, it was our act. We got out there and we both froze. You know well we were never on the — I was never on the stage and the damn stage, the people were — so I ran up the stairs and I ran right into a little girl’s dressing room. So they pushed me back on to the stage. By the time I got back my cousin was gone, he must have took off. So I don’t know what I did. I know I went — so they gave us ice cream, that was the end. But © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

that was the first time I was ever in front of an audience you know. And from then, then he got me a mandolin for a little while. I didn’t like it. It isn’t that I didn’t like it, I didn’t know what to do with it. Then he got me a banjo. And I’ve still got the banjo.
Still the same one?
Yeah that he bought. It was about a hundred dollars, so it was a Weymann banjo, and it’s a great banjo, but I’ve used it all these years.
And a hundred dollars at that time was significant.
It was a lot, yeah. And he thought because I could do these things.
But did it ever get to the point where all of a sudden your father was saying now wait a minute, this music stuff is okay for fun—

Oh yeah, yeah. Well then after he got me the banjo, then he got me a teacher in a candy store. The guy owned a candy store and I’d go back there and he’d show me. But he did do one thing. I had two banjo teachers. And they at least tried to make you learn how to read music. You know it wasn’t like C or nothing like that, it was written out and you had to learn where everything is. Now they have all the, like Harry Reser’s, he was a popular band leader, Cliquot Eskimos I think they were called. Harry Reser, he played like a violin player would play, you know, those banjo solos. So I had that environment, which I try to tell these kids that helped me out because at least I saw music in front of me. Where some of them now, they just see G seventh, and then — well now they’re coming to me, they come to me and they say what’s that called, what’s that called. Oh what’s a flat nine, what’s a — I says wait a minute. Flat nine. I says you know the old Italian guy, he comes in, he’s sitting on his porch, he’s just got done playing with the grapes all day long, his hands are all cut and callused. And he sits on his porch, he has his bottle of wine there, and he drinks a couple of wines and he picks up his guitar and he goes [scats]. If you can’t do that, forget it. You know what I mean? Like make it that everybody’s dancing and singing music. You know what I mean? You know what the first question I ask them after they get all through telling me they played with this Rock group and that group. I says you want to learn how to read? They say yeah, that’s why I came, I want you to, I heard that you make me read. I says well what’s a note? You don’t want me to ask you.
What’s a note?
Yeah, what’s a note?
What’s a note. Well it’s a duration of sound.

Well that’s close. But they either say it’s a pitch or something like that. What it is is a set of regular vibrations. A musical note. See if it isn’t set, it isn’t musical. And that goes, and it has four elements. So I says that’s all I talk about. When you’re talking and playing for me, I’m picking your weakest one and I’m showing you what your weaknesses are. © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-
So I say what are they? They don’t know. I say what’s a musical tone? I don’t want to embarrass you.
What’s a musical tone?
Yeah. A note represents a musical tone.
All right. Well a tone has pitch.
That’s one.
It has length.
That’s called duration.
Duration. Yes. It has volume.
Dynamics.
Dynamics, okay.
Very good.
And it has — oh boy — inflection?
Well timbre. It’s the sound, the sound.
The particular sound of that.

Yeah. It could be two instruments — well it could be the same instrument and you’ve got to get your sound to come out. That’s why you know like if I take a guitar player, you know, and I’ve got a French guy, he come over from France. And he’s a Django Reinhardt, he thinks he’s a Django Reinhardt. I says well that’s all right but you’re a traditionalist. So don’t forget, I told you you’re a traditionalist. I says a lot of the guys playing Dixieland, you know, they play Dixieland music. I say I’m not a traditionalist. I don’t care what you play. If you want to play you play. But a traditionalist would be somebody who’s staying like Dixieland or Django Reinhardt, like 50 years ago. But I seem to go from — wherever I go I seem to get in with other guys and I guess I’ve got some kind of a thing that I blend with them in some sort. I don’t hurt their playing. And that’s a big deal, I try to tell them.
That’s an important phrase right there. Don’t hurt their playing.

Oh well sure. That’s right. That’s why you might not play so good, but they play good. And I think Louis Armstrong, when I listen to Louis Armstrong, some of his early bands, I’d say gee why is he having a saxophone player, that guy, he don’t play that good you know. But now I realize that Louis could play good with these guys. You know, like if you get with some good players, sometimes they sound good but you feel them crowding you out.
Yeah. This is my date.
Yeah.
Well anyway, you pursued the banjo for a while. How did you get into the guitar, and what time was that? © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

Well now the banjo I kept going because I had my own radio show, like I didn’t get paid for it, but it was WHN like in Loew’s State building. I was there for six months all alone, no piano or anything. I just played these solos.
Did you sing too?
No.
Just banjo solo. Wow.

I wish I would have taped some of it you know. Well anyway, from there I got in with some bands, like one was in the Pelham East Theater. I think that’s where, that’s in the Bronx, and that was like they had a girlie show, and we had the violin player was the leader and he played C melody sax. And we had a tenor sax, two tenor saxes, a trumpet player, piano, drums. No bass. And me on banjo. But guitar was coming in. So I got a guitar but I couldn’t hear the guitar. I mean because there was no mic. So I couldn’t hear the guitar, so what I did I went out and I bought I think they call it a dobro. It’s got a metal plate in it. It was a National guitar. Dobro?
Oh, dobro.

Yeah that’s it. But I didn’t know it. I thought it was — but I could hear it a little better because I had this resonator in it I guess you’d call it. So whenever I’d get like a tune that was in C or G, I’d pick the guitar up, and eventually, little by little, the banjo was out and the guitar was in. See I used the banjo because I used to go on in the floor show I’d play “Stars and Stripes Forever” or something like that. But then the banjo went out and I just got to know the guitar. I didn’t take lessons right away on it, but I did have the advantage of reading music from the banjo, so I was trying to find that on the guitar you know, which some of these fellas don’t have.
Can you recall what kind of money you were making on those first engagements with this band?

Well it’s different areas. When I first went out I was, there was days when everything was illegal. There was no liquor, so it was prohibition. So everything I went with, even club dates, if they served liquor illegal so the girls, we used to have a kitty. And we’d have three pieces, like a drummer, banjo and saxophone, that was it. And the girls would pass the band and say, “Hey, play ‘Melancholy Baby.’” And they’d give them a tip. So they’d throw — so one night I come home and I had twenty-five dollars on my dresser. Oh I didn’t get paid twenty-five dollars, I got paid something like three or four dollars. But if it was a good night with these girls, and everybody was drinking, then all the girls got them drunk, the more they — So my father woke me up, he says, “Where’d you get that money?” Because he was only making about forty five dollars a week. So I tell him, I says we had a very good night. There was a couple of guys there and they just kept on giving us tips, so that was my end, we made seventy-five dollars in tips, which was a © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

good night. So anyway, but the average job was about four, five dollars, you know, that was a job. But when I had my own group, they picketed the place. The union was coming in then, Petrillo. So the boss didn’t want the picket lines around the place. So he says join the union. So the guy comes in who was the head picketer, he says, “All right, so what do we have to do to join the union the boss asks.” And so he says they each have to give twenty-five dollars. And you’ve got to come down and see if you read. But because you’ve got a job, you don’t have to come down, give us the twenty-five dollars. Well they were trying to get in, and we were working. So on that job when it became legal, I was the leader, I made thirty-five dollars. Seven nights a week. And no hours. You got there at nine o’clock. But if there was people there at 3:30 —
You just kept playing.

Yeah. And seven nights too. And the guys would make twenty-five dollars see. And like I tell the guys, like that’s where I got most of my training, because when you sit like six and seven hours a night, seven days a week and you just play, by the end of the night, you get so relaxed with playing. Because there was hardly any rest. Like you’d play, and then a girlie would go on and sing or dance or something, and then you’d play another for the dancing, and then another one. So you had the instrument. So I said you poor guys, you don’t have that advantage. The only thing you can do is get around with each others in the house, or play with the records. I says but this was like a thing.
That was like school for you.

Oh, you can’t buy that. Even sitting in, that’s what they’re trying to do, but it isn’t as regular as that. You know like and generally it would wind up to be a lot of cutting, you know, this guy plays this. And this place I ran, I had noted, my theme song was “No Sitting In at the Sherwood Inn.” Well I mean Friday and Saturday, and every night I had a different band. Like I had a different drummer, different bass player, and whatever the horn player was. And everybody came there, like Milt Hinton, Bobby Hackett, Clark Terry, all of them, Zoot, Al, they all came. Lee Konitz came.
And this was where? At the Sherwood Inn?
Yeah. That was in New Hyde Park, right near where I live. I had everybody there.
Can I take you back just a few years — you were a teenager during the depression?
Well I was just about — what year was the depression?
The depression was mid-30s.
‘38 or something like that? I don’t think I was a teenager. I remember my father, he went out selling apples for a nickel a piece. That’s how he had to make enough. Because it got so bad.
Did he lose his job during that time? © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

No, no he didn’t lose — I guess he did lose his job because that’s all he was doing. See he wound up to be — the whole family was printers outside of me. So his father wanted him to be a printer, and he became a printer. But then his father was older with his father’s brother, it was an uncle I guess of mine, but I didn’t know him very much, but they were old-time. And my grandfather couldn’t get along with his brother. And they had a fight. So that means my father and him were out. So my grandfather, he didn’t have no business then. And he went to work for a newspaper, I think it was the Bronx Home or North Side News, which eventually became the Bronx Home News. And don’t forget, my father went to the ninth — I went to the ninth grade elementary school, I quit. My father went to sixth grade and he quit. My grandfather went to the first grade. One year and he quit and he went to work. And you know what he wound up to be? A proofreader in a newspaper. Well you know why because you learn on the job. I tell these stories because that’s why I try to tell them, that’s what I did with music you know. See because he said you know like what makes Sammy run, I think there was a story like that, you know, like he just worked around the newspaper, picked up all the trash, and all of a sudden, well that’s what my grandfather did, but he did learn how to print because you see them setting type and then you learn, you didn’t even know you were learning how to read and write. Well that’s the best way to learn.
That’s a great story. I had something about you playing with a fellow named Jerry Wald?

Jerry Wald. He thought he was — after a while, when I first got with him he was imitating Hal Kemp, the clarinet would be in megaphones with their hands through and it’s a lot to get out of that kind of music [scats], but then Artie Shaw retired and Jerry got the big idea, so nearly overnight he got all of his arrangements, and the whole band changed. Then it was supposed to be like Artie Shaw you know. Yeah I worked with him in the Spanish Gardens in New York, did a broadcast, you know we were on, I guess every night they did the Band of America or something, they’d jump like a half hour in this place and then they’d be out in California. All the big bands would get a shot out there every night. I did it with Abe Lyman too.
What age were you when you moved away, moved out of your family house?

At 14 years old I had my own radio show. I was working in these speakeasies and things like that. Then a big out of town job came along, which was out in Far Rockaway. But you know I had to live out. Is that what you mean?
Yes.

When I moved out of the house. Yeah, so I went down to Rockaway and I stayed down there for almost a year. And from then on, when I did go home, I was always working. I’d just come in, say hello. And I was on the road with different bands. It was very early like, I didn’t even know that I was young. The guys who were working, they’d call me © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-
the big shot, to kid, they’d kid, he’s a big shot. And I didn’t know what the hell they were talking about. Evidently they thought I was someone.
Right. Can I assume that your father eventually came to terms with your life as a musician?

Well he wanted me to get a real job. That’s what he classed it as. So I said gee, I like what I’m doing. He said yeah but you’ve got to get a real job, you’re getting too old. I was about 18 or 17. He says you’ve got to get a job. He says come on down to the shop with me. So he brought me all the way down to 11th Street, down in New York where we are, and it was in the summer, and that means I had to take a trolley car to the subway, the subway and then I had to walk a couple of blocks you see, on a hot summer’s day. No air conditioner. He opened the door to get into this big shop, it was Vannery’s Press, it was, by the way he started off just picking up bags and everything. He wound up to be the foreman of this big print shop. You know they made big books like Bibles and things like that, it was Vannery’s Press. He opened this door and the ink, the smell of ink hit me and I almost passed out. I said Pop, I can’t make it. I couldn’t see myself going there. So then he kept after me. You know he says geez, you’ve got to get something. So one of my friends who was a leader of one of the club date bands, he worked in Celanese, it’s an imitation silk, but it was just starting, so he says they’re hiring guys. I know how old I was, I was 16 at that time. Because NRA came in, and you got, it was $16 you were allowed to make, or you had to make $16 a week. So I went in to this Celanese, and after about six months the boss called me in and he says, “Hey, I hear you’re a musician.” I said, “Yeah, I play banjo and guitar.” He says, “I’m a banjo player.” He says, “Do me a favor. You take your lunch hour and then you come back and you come in my office.” So I got talking to him there, and he says, “What the hell are you doing here anyway?” I says, “Because my father wants to see why I don’t work, so I’m going to hold a job for six months or a year to show him I can do it.” So he says, “Yeah but this job ain’t nothing.” He says, “You see them guys pushing them things around” the rolls of silk and whatever. He says, “They’ve been here for ten years.” He says, “Every year I give them a buck or two bucks raise.” He says, “They’re married.” He says, “You, so far in six months,” he says, “I had you in the receiving clerk, you know, you’re feeding the machines, double and fold machine,“ he says, “I give you everything, opening the crates,” he says, “and you could do it.” He says, “They can’t do anything.” I’ve got to keep them on the same job” he says. So then he offered me a job in the underwear department because the underwear department was new at Celanese. Am I boring you?
No.

The underwear department was just starting. So the old guy who was the head of it, he got sick. So he says, “You go down there,” and he says, “we’re going crazy. Every time © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-

this guy don’t come in, nobody can get any orders because he’s got like a 42 blue over there, then he’s got a 42 blue up there, and he’s got it so mixed up that nobody can, it’s all mixed up.” He says, “Will you go down there and condense the stock?” I said, “I don’t know what you mean, condense.” He says, “Well you know, put all the blues together and the sizes together.” I said okay. So I went down there and it was only a little room, it was just like here but bigger than that. So I put everything in order and I was sitting there. He come by and he says, “What’s the matter, where are you, why aren’t you working?” I said, “Well what do you want me to do?” He says, “I told you, condense.” I says, “I did.” So he comes in, and he looked at it and he says, “Hey, you want this job?” He says, “This job pays $35.” And that was a lot of money, because he was only making about $60 at that time. He says, “And it’s going to be big, you’ll have guys under you.”
And you were 16?
Wow.

And you did it, yeah.

Yeah, so they keep on saying. I says well why don’t you do it? I can’t help it. You know what I mean? And they are good, but maybe it’s this other quality, that I can get along with these people. Just like we’re sitting here talking, you don’t feel any strain to make me talk, do you?
No certainly not.
Can I have all the outtakes? How long is that?
We can wrap up pretty soon here, because I know you have to get going. Here’s a hard question maybe. How’s that for an introduction?

Yeah wait a minute, that’s what Phil Schaap says. I was talking to him and we got going, and he says, “I’m going to look that up,” he says, “you’ve got me worried.” He says, “I used to think I knew everything, but when you questioned it—” and that same program after I got back, Jimmy Hall rang me up, and he says, “Me and my wife were out in the country and I heard you being interviewed.” He says, “Man,” he says, “when I was being interviewed, this guy would get me so wrapped up I couldn’t talk.” He knew everything. He says he was getting it.
Well maybe it’s time for another book, huh?
No, one is enough. I’ve got a lot of things I could—
What do you think is the—
Why don’t you write a book?
I think it will. Especially after today.

You should. Everybody should. Everybody should. You know like I tell the guys I says make a diary, every day. I’ve got a little machine, you know, you just, when you think of a story just tell the machine. And at the end of a week or so, copy all of them down. That’s what I more or less did.
You’ll have a lot of material in a hurry, yeah. © Fillius Jazz Archive -23-
Well I just kept on putting it down on a little cassette or something. You should. You’ve got a great name, Monk.
I’ve got that going for me. Well do you remember a particular—
And Rowe you know, you know, you know—
Now I forgot my question.

When we were down in the village, this is before I met any of them guys, maybe I knew Flip, but then we had a trio, a bass, a piano and a guitar. That was like a big hot trio. Carl Senior was the piano player. But Bob Rowe was the bass player. And Bob Rowe — this was down on Bleecker Street and it’s right on the corner, it’s still a bar, and a wild little place.
In the village.

Yeah. Everybody came in and sit in with this little trio. Bob Rowe had three strings on his bass. It was a three string bass. To this day I’ve never seen one. And he also played a little guitar, he was sort of a Django Reinhardt type. But anyway, well I didn’t mean to get off, but he had your last name. And he wound up to be the principal bass player in the New Orleans Symphony. Me and my wife went out there when I was on the road, and I looked him up. And him and his wife, Dotty, who he was going — she sent him to Juilliard, and she worked as a waitress and let him go to Juilliard, and he became a classical bass player. Very intelligent guy too. But he took us out there and it was a groovy night in New Orleans. First he took us out — first we’d have like some kind of soup and crabs or something, in one place. Then we’d go to another place and have some kind of fish. Then we’d go to another place and have our dessert. In the meantime we were walking all over, it took the whole night, just going to different kinds of places. Pretty groovy.
It sounds like a swinging town.
Yeah. Well that’s where he wound up.
Can you think of when one of the hardest recordings you ever participated in? Would it have been some of the more modern stuff? Or don’t you even look at it that way?
You mean when I got tied up inside. Well there was a couple of times. With Stravinsky, forget about it.
Tell me about that, will you, the Stravinsky?
Was it Stravinsky or Stokowski? Stokowski. The conductor.
Oh, Stokowski, yes.
At NBC.
Oh, yeah, at NBC.
But the other one—
Stravinsky wrote the piece for Woody Herman. © Fillius Jazz Archive -24-

Yeah but he just come back — he got us together in maybe a half hour. We were trying to play it, we couldn’t. Because it wasn’t just the rhythms. Everybody had different little things you know. But he come in and clapped his hands like this [claps]. And we all gathered, and he says — the classical guys were telling him what to do.
Yeah. Stokowski.

But one of my hardest things, well this wasn’t in the book so I could tell you, like it was a band with strings and everything, a commercial date, but with strings and everything, it was very fast. And the guitar had to play all afterbeats. And in the middle I’d get mixed up. It was long, like about four or five minutes, and they had the guitar piped up. No piano, just bass and drums and this guitar had to get that afterbeat. That’s tough. I mean very fast too. And he’d stop and he’d say, “You’re very important.” I finally got it. He says, “That’s all right.” Well that’s hard. Like it wasn’t a ridiculous thing to do—
If you got off once, all of a sudden you’re on the downbeats instead of the ups.
Oh that happened down in the village with Jacques Brel’s “Alive and Dead” or “Dead and Alive” whatever.
Oh yes. “Alive and Well.”

Yes. They had a little quartet down there. And Wayne Wright sent me in as a sub. And I got along all right. But there was seven-eight time and things like that you know. And the keyboard player didn’t play piano, he played all kinds of, what the hell they call it. The drummer was never, never just rhythm, just me and the bass. I think Teddy Kotick was the bass player. So there was one in seven-eight time. Again I had the afterbeats. And it was one, zing, one, zing, one, zing zing. One, zing, one, zing— And so it was all right the first show. Then we had a little time off, like the matinee, and we’d come back for that. In the meantime we’d go out and have a couple of drinks. It was funny. You know like little things like that, you figure you get all messed up with the big bunch of things, but the little things like this, they’re so — well of course it’s hard to be simple.
It’s hard to be simple in seven-eight.

Well that’s what I tell the guys, I says you know you’re always looking all over the place and really it’s right next to you. Like the upper and lower neighborhood. I mean they’re looking all over and it’s right next to them. You know like if you played a D flat seven to a C to make it. It’s a substitution, but no they’d be looking all over. Well.
Did we just run out of a tape?
We must have.
Okay, we’ll wrap up here. Who do you listen to these days? Do you listen to any particular younger players?

I listen to — see the way I do it, I tell them, they come to me as a teacher. I says I’m not a teacher, I’m an instructor. You’re the teacher. If you can’t teach yourself, you know I tell © Fillius Jazz Archive -25-
you to do this, you keep doing this, and if you can’t do it, then you can’t teach yourself. So if you don’t like me then don’t come to me. But you go on your own. So what was the question?
Talking about listening, if you have any favorites that you listen to now?

No, what I do, I generally let them hear like I say, like if they sing sometimes I put “So What” on. Mainly I put that on, well it’s the record, but it mainly is that if I’m showing them the Dorian mode say, it’s a good example, because all they have to do is play in one key and then go up a half a tone higher, and back. So I get them, that they start to hear it, like that’s all, and then I analyze some of [scats] see and I show them that that’s only a couple of notes in the scale. So if he can do it you can. You know, like why are you running all over for? You know that’s what I like, sort of. Anyway, what are we talking about again? Oh, showing them how simple, and why scales are important. Like if I say that’s the Dorian mode, well man, the whole record they hardly play anything but the Dorian mode. Like when you analyze it, oh a couple of times they play a little out of the way.
But they come back in.

Yeah, yeah, yeah. Like see for one here, you know when you argue with me why do I have to know my scales, that’s why. And I can talk to you. I says like I explain that. When they argue with me, I says, “I know you don’t have to know it,” I says, “But you’re looking at a guy who happens to have everything else.” I says, “You’re like Tal Farlow. He don’t practice scales, it’s true.” I says, “But you whistle a scale and here Tal was right with you.” I says that’s the difference, you can’t do that.
Well it sounds like your students are fortunate to be working with you, I would say that.
Well I’ve got some guys that were hanging around me for 20 years. You know they don’t come every week, but they’ll take a year off and then they’ll ring up, “I need a little brush up.”
Well this has really been a pleasure for me to talk to you, and I appreciate—
I hope you think so when you see it.
I hope so too.
Maybe this will be it. Thanks for coming, I hope it’s not snowing. You know of all the days that it snowed, it didn’t snow, I don’t think it snowed the whole winter.
Right. Just our luck.
A blizzard.
Right. Well thanks for your time. I hope you have a safe trip back, and you’ve had a marvelous career and I appreciate your sharing it with me today.

I’m glad, I mean I have no, you know like if you ask me what would I do, I don’t think I could do anything else. I enjoyed it most of the time, most of the time I enjoyed it. I © Fillius Jazz Archive -26-
wasn’t begrudging anybody, I wasn’t mad at somebody because they did it better. I mean I don’t look at life that way.
Right.
This is the way I did it and that’s why I’m telling you to write a book, him, the guy that’s taking all these pictures, he should write a book. Everybody. Like what else is there to do?
Okay.
So a hundred years from now somebody, if they’re fortunate, they’ll be able to see.
They’ll be able to see it. All right.
Well bye bye.
Thanks for your time. © Fillius Jazz Archive -27-

segments.title: Copyright statement and biographical note
segments.summary: Archive copyright notice and a short biography of Billy Bauer.

segments.title: Opening of the filming session
segments.summary: Monk Rowe introduces Bauer on a snowy morning and asks about his guitar school.

segments.title: Teaching guitar: finger patterns versus knowing the notes
segments.summary: Bauer describes his small school, urging students to sing the lines of players like Lester Young and to learn where notes are on the fingerboard; about eighteen students and a weakened voice from singing with them.

segments.title: Don't imitate: fingerprints, and being a sideman
segments.summary: He tells students they can never sound like anyone else, then reflects that he was a sideman all his life, as the title of his book says.

segments.title: Making your own record date, then versus now
segments.summary: Rowe asks if he would have made his own record at 21; Bauer says no, recalling a time with only an old victrola.

segments.title: Born in the Bronx; family singing and his father's amateur nights
segments.summary: Born in 1915 in the Bronx, he grew up in a household where everyone sang; his father performed on amateur nights and vaudeville.

segments.title: Prices of movies, vaudeville and club dates
segments.summary: Movie and vaudeville ticket prices, and a comparison with what young players earn on club dates today.

segments.title: Father the printer; ukulele, mandolin and the Weymann banjo
segments.summary: His father, a printer who nearly made Broadway, gave him a ukulele when he broke his leg at nine; the stage-fright debut led to a mandolin and a banjo he still owns.

segments.title: Banjo teachers, learning to read, and what a note is
segments.summary: Two banjo teachers made him read music; he now asks students what a note is, answering that it is a set of regular vibrations with four elements.

segments.title: Tone elements, traditionalists, and not hurting other players
segments.summary: The four elements of a tone; he calls himself no traditionalist and says his gift is blending without crowding other players, as Louis Armstrong's sidemen did.

segments.title: Radio show on WHN and the move from banjo to guitar
segments.summary: He kept the banjo for a solo radio show on WHN, then in a Bronx theater band bought a resonator guitar and gradually switched, helped by his banjo reading.

segments.title: Prohibition-era pay, tips, the union, and the Sherwood Inn
segments.summary: Early jobs paid a few dollars but tips could be large; as leader he earned $35 a week seven nights after the union came in, and he later ran the Sherwood Inn in New Hyde Park.

segments.title: The Depression and his father and grandfather in printing
segments.summary: His father sold apples in the Depression; Bauer recounts the family's printing trade and how his grandfather learned on the job.

segments.title: Playing with Jerry Wald
segments.summary: Wald first imitated Hal Kemp and then remade the band in Artie Shaw's style; they broadcast from the Spanish Gardens.

segments.title: Leaving home at fourteen for Far Rockaway
segments.summary: At fourteen, with his own radio show and speakeasy work, he moved to Far Rockaway and was soon on the road.

segments.title: Father's push for a real job: print shop and Celanese
segments.summary: His father took him to the print shop but the ink smell overwhelmed him; he took a job at Celanese while playing nights, and a kind boss, Mr. Keyes, let him sleep in the back.

segments.title: Phil Schaap radio interview in a snowstorm
segments.summary: Bauer recalls a marathon radio interview with Phil Schaap that ran for hours during a snowstorm.

segments.chapter: Woody Herman and the war years
segments.title: How he joined Woody Herman
segments.summary: Woody phoned him; he signed a contract and flew to join the band, where he already knew Flip Phillips and Davy Tough joined at the same time.

segments.chapter: Woody Herman and the war years
segments.title: Earlier big bands, reading double stops, and tablature
segments.summary: He had played with Wald, Abe Lyman and Carl Hoff, brushed up his reading for Hoff's book, and objects to tablature; he also mentions current students.

segments.chapter: Woody Herman and the war years
segments.title: USO work and a near assignment to South America
segments.summary: In Abe Lyman's band he did USO shows; he was nearly sent as a quasi-spy musician to a neutral South American country.

segments.chapter: Woody Herman and the war years
segments.title: Harlem after hours and the term offay
segments.summary: He recalls the Herman band's swing, and Black musicians taking him to Minton's and Harlem bars, where Slingshot explained hijive talk.

segments.title: Freddie Green and Manny's golf day with Clark Terry
segments.summary: At Manny's annual musicians' golf outing Freddie Green talked to him and he made a bet with Clark Terry; later a limousine meeting with Terry.

segments.title: Touring with Herman: Army bases, a stripped plane and San Diego
segments.summary: Travel by bus, train and a bare cargo plane with parachutes; in San Diego the band lived out of town to avoid servicemen.

segments.title: The Herman rhythm section: Chubby Jackson and Davy Tough
segments.summary: Chubby's shouting drove the section while Davy Tough was not flashy; Flip says Davy took his only solo on Bauer's tune.

segments.title: Listening to Skyscraper with Flip Phillips
segments.summary: They play a recording of the tune Bauer wrote, with Davy Tough's four-bar solo, and talk about the record.

segments.title: Getting Flip Phillips into Abe Lyman's band
segments.summary: Bauer recommended Flip to Lyman; he explains how hotel residencies and radio worked for bands.

segments.title: Chubby Jackson and Sonny Berman roughhousing
segments.summary: Chubby knocked down Sonny Berman and Bauer in horseplay; Bauer says Chubby played with the same unsophisticated drive.

segments.title: Davy Tough and Max Roach on keeping the groove
segments.summary: Davy Tough and Max Roach each pushed the band to a place and stayed there, which Bauer says makes a good band.

segments.title: Small group with Chubby Jackson and Lennie Tristano
segments.summary: A short-lived group clashed: Lennie wanted him not to play rhythm while Chubby pushed ahead, with Arnold Fishkin on bass.

segments.title: Driving lesson for Lennie Tristano and his games
segments.summary: Bauer let Tristano drive his car at 3 a.m. and recalls his skill at bar games.

segments.title: Sideman humility: Ralph Burns, Neal Hefti and the Pam ending
segments.summary: He says he only stayed out of musicians' way, and that Ralph Burns and Shorty Rogers fixed the ending of Pam without telling him.

segments.chapter: Metronome All Stars and Charlie Parker
segments.title: Metronome All Stars and the call from Charlie Parker
segments.summary: He describes Parker, Miles and Dizzy in the All Stars, and wishing aloud for Bird to call him; Bird phoned within weeks.

segments.chapter: Metronome All Stars and Charlie Parker
segments.title: Phil Schaap, Jimmy Hall and writing a book
segments.summary: Phil Schaap questioned his facts, and Bauer urges Rowe and everybody to keep a diary or write a book.

segments.chapter: Metronome All Stars and Charlie Parker
segments.title: Bob Rowe and the Bleecker Street trio
segments.summary: Prompted by Rowe's name, he recalls a Village trio with bassist Bob Rowe, who later played in New Orleans and hosted a night out.

segments.title: Hardest dates: Stravinsky or Stokowski, and a string date with afterbeats
segments.summary: He recalls Herman's Stravinsky piece and Stokowski at NBC, then a fast string date requiring all afterbeats.

segments.title: Jacques Brel show in the Village and keeping it simple
segments.summary: Subbing in the Brel quartet he played afterbeats in seven-eight; he says it is hard to be simple.

segments.title: Tape change; teaching with So What, Dorian mode and scales
segments.summary: After a tape change, he uses So What to show the Dorian mode and why scales matter, citing Tal Farlow.

segments.title: Closing thoughts and goodbyes
segments.summary: Thanks, reflections on enjoying a career without envy, and goodbye.
